name: LifeWire CivClock Circadian Precision Implant
description:
The CivClock is a low-power circadian and precision alarm implant seated just beneath the skin of the inner wrist, wrapped around the radial nerve pathway. It interfaces with the body's existing sleep-wake hormonal cycle — primarily melatonin and cortisol rhythms — to track sleep stages in real time and deliver a calibrated haptic and mild neurochemical nudge at the exact desired wake moment. Rather than forcing the body awake mid-deep-sleep cycle (the hallmark misery of legacy alarm technology), the CivClock monitors sleep phase depth and wakes the user at the lightest natural point within a user-defined window, typically fifteen minutes. Alarm delivery is a gentle warmth in the wrist accompanied by a subtle elevation in cortisol that mimics the body's natural pre-dawn rise. No sound, no light, no external device required. The system is configurable via any standard BCI interface, or through a companion app for those without neural mesh.

The CivClock is one of the most commonly installed pieces of cyberware in Meridian 88, so ubiquitous among Tier 2 and Tier 3 workers that owning an external alarm clock is considered mildly eccentric. Shift workers in the manufacturing belts of the Shelf rely on it heavily — missing a shift start can cost a day's wages or worse, and the CivClock's phase-aware wake system means they arrive alert rather than groggy. Parents use it to sync household wake schedules silently. Students set multiple study alarms without disturbing dormitory neighbors. The sensation of waking without an external device — simply opening your eyes at the exact right moment — is something users consistently describe as one of the quiet dignities of modern life.
installation_requirements: Outpatient pharmacy kiosk or walk-in clinic; 20-minute procedure under local anesthetic, no specialist required
maintenance: Firmware update annually via BCI sync or kiosk terminal; passive kinetic charging via wrist movement, no battery replacement needed; optional sleep-cycle recalibration every two years
specifications: {"wake_window_resolution": "±90 seconds of target time", "sleep_stage_tracking": "4-stage via cortisol/melatonin sampling", "alarm_delivery": "haptic + mild cortisol elevation", "power_source": "kinetic microgenerator, radial movement", "battery_reserve": "72-hour passive reserve", "connectivity": "BCI mesh optional, standalone capable", "alarm_slots": "up to 24 programmable", "form_factor": "4mm subdermal node, 12mm sensor ribbon"}
side_effects: Mild tingling at wrist installation site during first two weeks
Occasional vivid, structured dreams during initial sleep-phase calibration period
Rare users report a faint sense of anticipation minutes before a scheduled alarm triggers
Minor skin discoloration at node site in very fair-skinned individuals, typically fades within a month
cultural_context: The CivClock carries essentially no social stigma — it is, in the parlance of Meridian 88, a 'baseline implant,' the kind of thing a parent gets installed in a teenager alongside their first civic ID chip. In Tier 1 and Tier 2 communities, not having one is more noteworthy than having one. Among Spire residents it's considered pedestrian, something the help has, though many Tier 4 and 5 citizens use premium versions under different brand names. There is a small countercultural movement — mostly in artistic communities in the Shelf's lower districts — that rejects circadian implants as 'corponation time' and insists on waking naturally, a stance most working people find impractical and faintly romantic.
known_users: anyone who has ever missed an alarm they couldn't afford to miss
story_hooks: A runner's CivClock has been remotely hacked to wake them three hours early every night for a week — sleep deprivation as sabotage, and no external device to trace
A murder victim's CivClock logged a wake alarm that never triggered — suggesting they were already dead before their scheduled 0400 shift start, contradicting the official time of death
A Tier 1 labor organizer is distributing bootleg CivClock firmware that encodes secret meeting times as alarm patterns — management is trying to identify who's carrying the modified signal
